subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: share the care schedule with siblings and relatives [Action]

Day 1. Vaibhav spread a large sheet on the dining table and drew a grid of seven days. Hospital stays, medicine pickups and cooking, each in a colour. Mum's care had been falling on him alone for weeks, and his eyes were sore from studying at night.

Day 4. He phoned his brother Jomon, his Masi and a neighbour. Jomon took Monday and Thursday nights at the hospital, Masi took Tuesday's cooking, and the neighbour offered to collect medicines on Saturdays. Vaibhav wrote each name in its slot.

Day 18. The rota had been followed for two weeks. He sat his exam with his mind clear and slept properly the night before. Mum said to him, softly, "You look better, beta."

How was Vaibhav feeling before he made the rota?
qa.a: Vaibhav was worn out and strained, shown by the sore eyes and the weeks of care falling on him alone.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav add to the rota to keep it working, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could set a fixed time each week to check that everyone is comfortable with their slots, because a shared plan needs small adjustments as things change.

qa.q: How might Mum see the new rota?
qa.a: Mum likely feels comforted that the family is sharing the care and relieved that Vaibhav is resting, as her remark on his looking better suggests.

"Sarita, you're carrying your Amma's care on your own, and it reminds me of when I was your age. Let me tell you what I did, and I'm Elizabeth, the one who learned the slow way.
My father had a stroke when I was in my last year of college. For a month I did everything: nights at the hospital, medicines, cooking for my younger brother, and then lectures. I fell asleep in an exam.
One evening I took a sheet of paper and drew a week. Hospital nights, medicine pickup, cooking. Then I phoned people. My brother took Tuesday and Thursday cooking. Aunt Mary did two hospital nights. Mr Pinto next door picked up medicines every Saturday. I stuck the sheet on the fridge.
It wasn't perfect. But I slept, and I passed. And Papa had more faces around him than just my tired one."

qa.q: Which days did Elizabeth's brother take for cooking?
qa.a: He took Tuesday and Thursday cooking.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel during the month of doing everything alone?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt exhausted and overstretched, to the point of falling asleep in an exam.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Elizabeth's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Drawing a week on paper and phoning people for fixed slots was the turning point, because it turned vague help into clear jobs others could do.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's father have experienced the change?
qa.a: Elizabeth's father likely felt comforted and less of a burden, with more faces around him than one tired one.

grounding: Shows a student writing a weekly care rota and asking a sibling, an aunt and a neighbour to take fixed slots so one person does not burn out.

Jasleen's phone had a cracked screen and nine percent battery when she sat down in the hospital corridor to make the rota. Her mother would be in for at least another week, the power had been going off at home every evening, and her final-term assignments were due Friday.
She drew seven boxes in her notebook. Nights at the hospital, medicine pickup, cooking for Nani, who lived with them.
Then she used the battery carefully. She called her brother Harman first: "You take Monday, Wednesday and Friday nights." Then Masi: "Can you cook Tuesdays and Thursdays?" Masi said yes before she finished. Her last call was to Dilnaz aunty from the flat below: "Could you pick up medicines on Saturday mornings?"
The phone died after the third call. Jasleen tore out the page and taped it to the nurses' notice board for the family to photograph. That night, for the first time in a week, she slept at home.

qa.q: How much battery did Jasleen's phone have when she started?
What was Jasleen likely feeling when she began making the rota?
qa.a: She was likely exhausted and pressured, with her mother in hospital, power cuts at home and assignments due Friday.

qa.q: What else could Jasleen do if one person drops a slot?
qa.a: She could name a back-up for each task on the same page, so one missed day doesn't fall back on her alone.

qa.q: How might Masi feel being asked to cook?
qa.a: Masi seems glad to help, saying yes before Jasleen even finished, perhaps relieved to have a clear way to be useful.

grounding: Shows a student writing a weekly care rota and asking a sibling, an aunt and a neighbour to take fixed slots, despite little time and battery.
